learningObjectives.title: Uses and dangers of EM waves

questions.q: What is the activity of a radioactive source?
options: The rate at which its nuclei decay, measured in becquerel (Bq)
The number of undecayed nuclei remaining
The energy of each emitted particle
The mass of the source
questions.explain: Activity is the rate at which nuclei of a source decay, measured in becquerel (Bq), where 1 Bq is one decay per second.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most strongly ionising but the least penetrating?
options: Alpha
Beta
Gamma
They are all equal
questions.explain: Alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising but least penetrating — it is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air.

questions.q: A nucleus undergoes alpha decay. How do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number −4, atomic number −2
Mass number −2, atomic number −4
Mass number stays the same, atomic number +1
Mass number −4, atomic number +2
questions.explain: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He, so the nucleus loses 4 from its mass number and 2 from its atomic number.

questions.q: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: The time for the source to completely decay
The time for the number of undecayed nuclei to halve
The time for the activity to double
Half the age of the sample
questions.explain: Half-life is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to halve (equivalently for its activity/count-rate to halve).

questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
options: Irradiation means a radioactive material gets onto or into an object; contamination means being exposed to radiation from a source
Irradiation means being exposed to radiation from a source; contamination means having radioactive atoms on or inside an object
They are exactly the same thing
Contamination only happens with gamma radiation
questions.explain: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source (the object does not become radioactive). Contamination is when radioactive atoms get onto or inside an object, which then continues to emit radiation.

questions.q: In a transverse wave, how do the oscillations relate to the direction the wave travels (energy transfer)?
options: Parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Perpendicular (at 90°) to the direction of energy transfer
In the same direction as the energy
There are no oscillations
questions.explain: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. In a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it.

questions.q: On a transverse wave diagram, what is the amplitude?
options: The distance between two adjacent peaks
The maximum displacement from the rest (undisturbed) position
The number of waves per second
The total length of the wave
questions.explain: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its rest position. The distance between adjacent peaks is the wavelength.

questions.q: Why does light bend (refract) when it passes from air into glass?
options: Its frequency changes
Its speed changes, which changes its direction (unless it hits the boundary along the normal)
It is absorbed
It speeds up in the glass
questions.explain: Refraction happens because the wave changes speed when it enters a different medium. Light slows down in glass; if it meets the boundary at an angle, this change of speed bends it toward the normal.

questions.q: What is the approximate range of frequencies that a healthy young human ear can hear?
options: 2 Hz to 200 Hz
20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
20 kHz to 20 MHz
0 Hz to 20 Hz
questions.explain: The normal human hearing range is about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz). Sound above this range is called ultrasound.

questions.q: Ultrasound is used for medical imaging (e.g. of a foetus). Which property of ultrasound makes this possible?
options: It is partially reflected at boundaries between different tissues/media
It is a type of light
It travels faster than X-rays
It is ionising
questions.explain: When ultrasound meets a boundary between two different media, some is reflected. The time for reflections to return is used to build an image. Ultrasound is non-ionising, making it safe for imaging.

questions.q: Which list shows the electromagnetic spectrum in order of INCREASING frequency?
options: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
Gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Radio, visible, microwave, X-ray, infrared, gamma, ultraviolet
Microwave, radio, infrared, visible, gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet
questions.explain: In order of increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength.

questions.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used for broadcasting television and radio signals over long distances?
options: Gamma rays
Radio waves
X-rays
Ultraviolet
questions.explain: Radio waves are used for TV and radio broadcasting. They have long wavelengths and can be transmitted, received and reflected over long distances.

questions.q: Which use is correctly matched to the EM wave?
options: Microwaves – cooking food and satellite communications
Infrared – sterilising surgical instruments
Gamma rays – TV remote controls
Radio waves – suntanning
questions.explain: Microwaves are used for cooking and satellite/mobile communications. Infrared is used in remote controls and heating; gamma rays sterilise equipment and treat cancer; UV causes tanning.

questions.q: A perfect black body is best described as an object that:
options: Reflects all radiation that hits it
Absorbs all the radiation that hits it and is also the best possible emitter
Only emits visible light
Cannot emit any radiation
questions.explain: A perfect black body absorbs all radiation incident on it and is also the best possible emitter of radiation. All bodies emit and absorb infrared (and other) radiation.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is described as a random process. What does this mean?
options: The source decays at a steady, predictable rate per nucleus
It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when
Decay only happens when the source is disturbed
All nuclei decay at exactly the same time
questions.explain: Decay is random: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay or when. A Geiger–Müller tube can measure the overall count-rate, but individual decays are unpredictable.

questions.q: Which material is needed to absorb (significantly reduce) gamma radiation?
options: A sheet of paper
A few millimetres of aluminium
Thick lead or several metres of concrete
A layer of air
questions.explain: Gamma is the most penetrating: paper stops alpha, a few mm of aluminium stops beta, but gamma needs thick lead or metres of concrete to reduce it significantly.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits a beta-minus particle, how does its atomic number change?
options: It decreases by 1
It increases by 1
It decreases by 2
It stays the same
questions.explain: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton (plus the emitted electron), so the mass number is unchanged but the atomic number increases by 1.

questions.q: A source has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 6 hours. What is its activity after 18 hours?
questions.explain: 18 hours = 3 half-lives. Activity halves each time: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq.

questions.q: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
options: A water wave
Light
A sound wave in air
A wave on a string
questions.explain: Sound is a longitudinal wave: the air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer, creating compressions and rarefactions.

questions.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 6.0 m. Calculate its wave speed.
When a wave is reflected from a flat surface, how does the angle of reflection compare with the angle of incidence (both measured from the normal)?
options: The angle of reflection is larger
The angle of reflection is smaller
They are equal
The wave is absorbed, not reflected
questions.explain: For reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal to the surface.

questions.q: Sound waves cause our eardrums to vibrate so we hear. Why can't sound travel through a vacuum?
options: A vacuum is too cold
There are no particles in a vacuum to vibrate and carry the wave
Sound is a transverse wave
A vacuum absorbs all sound
questions.explain: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs particles in a medium to oscillate and pass on the vibration. A vacuum has no particles, so sound cannot travel through it.

questions.q: An ultrasound pulse travels through tissue at 1500 m/s. It reflects off a boundary and returns to the probe after a total time of 0.0001 s. How deep is the boundary?
questions.explain: Total distance = speed × time = 1500 × 0.0001 = 0.15 m. The pulse travels there and back, so depth = 0.15 ÷ 2 = 0.075 m.

questions.q: How do all electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum?
options: At different speeds depending on frequency
All at the same speed (the speed of light)
They cannot travel through a vacuum
Only visible light can travel through a vacuum
questions.explain: All EM waves are transverse and travel at the same speed (about 3 × 10⁸ m/s) through a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength, not speed in a vacuum.
